Addressing the challenges of generating counterfactual explanations that reflect true cause/effect relationships rather than spurious correlations.
Exploring interactive and human-in-the-loop approaches to enhance causability and user understanding.
papers.abstract: There has been a growing interest in model-agnostic methods that can make deep learning models more transparent and explainable to a user. Some researchers recently argued that for a machine to achieve a certain degree of human-level explainability, this machine needs to provide human causally understandable explanations, also known as causability. A specific class of algorithms that have the potential to provide causability are counterfactuals. This paper presents an in-depth systematic review of the diverse existing body of literature on counterfactuals and causability for explainable artificial intelligence. We performed an LDA topic modelling analysis under a PRISMA framework to find the most relevant literature articles. This analysis resulted in a novel taxonomy that considers the grounding theories of the surveyed algorithms, together with their underlying properties and applications in real-world data. This research suggests that current model-agnostic counterfactual algorithms for explainable AI are not grounded on a causal theoretical formalism and, consequently, cannot promote causability to a human decision-maker. Our findings suggest that the explanations derived from major algorithms in the literature provide spurious correlations rather than cause/effects relationships, leading to sub-optimal, erroneous or even biased explanations. This paper also advances the literature with new directions and challenges on promoting causability in model-agnostic approaches for explainable artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Inducing Causal Structure for Interpretable Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we bring well-founded causal insights into neural models while still allowing them to learn in a data-driven fashion?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces interchange intervention training (IIT), a method to train neural networks to realize a target causal model, which improves interpretability and systematic generalization.
papers.conclusion: IIT is an effective method for inducing causal structure in neural networks, leading to improved interpretability and systematic generalization.
papers.key_findings:
IIT achieves the best results on systematic generalization tasks across three benchmarks.
IIT produces neural models that more successfully realize the target causal model, as measured by interchange intervention accuracy.
IIT combines effectively with multi-task objectives, further improving performance.
IIT guarantees that when the loss is zero, the target causal model is a causal abstraction of the neural network.
Without IIT, models fail to generalize on systematic generalization splits.
papers.limitation:
The symbolic causal structures and variable mappings are not unique and may not be optimal, and the choice of mapping affects performance.
The formulation of example pairs for IIT affects performance, which is left for future research.
future_direction: Investigate the effects of example pairing on model performance.
Explore optimal mappings between causal variables and neural representations.
papers.abstract: In many areas, we have well-founded insights about causal structure that would be useful to bring into our trained models while still allowing them to learn in a data-driven fashion. To achieve this, we present the new method of interchange intervention training (IIT). In IIT, we (1) align variables in a causal model (e.g., a deterministic program or Bayesian network) with representations in a neural model and (2) train the neural model to match the counterfactual behavior of the causal model on a base input when aligned representations in both models are set to be the value they would be for a source input. IIT is fully differentiable, flexibly combines with other objectives, and guarantees that the target causal model is a causal abstraction of the neural model when its loss is zero. We evaluate IIT on a structural vision task (MNIST-PVR), a navigational language task (ReaSCAN), and a natural language inference task (MQNLI). We compare IIT against multi-task training objectives and data augmentation. In all our experiments, IIT achieves the best results and produces neural models that are more interpretable in the sense that they more successfully realize the target causal model.

papers.title: Causality is Key for Interpretability Claims to Generalise
papers.research_question: How can interpretability claims be made more rigorous and generalizable? The paper argues that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures and the evidence needed to support such claims.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal framework for interpretability, arguing that claims should be stated in the language of causal inference and identifiability to ensure they generalize. It uses Pearl's causal hierarchy to diagnose claim-evidence mismatches and causal representation learning to specify assumptions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability claims should be grounded in causal inference to ensure they generalize, and practitioners should use a causal framework to align methods, evidence, and claims.
papers.key_findings:
There is a frequent gap between the evidence provided by interpretability methods (e.g., associational) and the strength of the claims made (e.g., interventional or counterfactual).
A pilot study of 50 papers found roughly half of interpretability claims can admit a stronger interpretation than the evidence supports, indicating a field-wide terminological challenge.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) has yielded important insights into model behaviour, yet recurring pitfalls persist: findings that do not generalise, and causal interpretations that outrun the evidence. Our position is that causal inference specifies what constitutes a valid mapping from model activations to invariant high-level structures, the data or assumptions needed to achieve it, and the inferences it can support. Specifically, Pearl's causal hierarchy clarifies what an interpretability study can justify. Observations establish associations between model behaviour and internal components. Interventions (e.g., ablations or activation patching) support claims how these edits affect a behavioural metric (\eg, average change in token probabilities) over a set of prompts. However, counterfactual claims -- i.e., asking what the model output would have been for the same prompt under an unobserved intervention -- remain largely unverifiable without controlled supervision. We show how causal representation learning (CRL) operationalises this hierarchy, specifying which variables are recoverable from activations and under what assumptions. Together, these motivate a diagnostic framework that helps practitioners select methods and evaluations matching claims to evidence such that findings generalise.

papers.title: iReason: Multimodal Commonsense Reasoning using Videos and Natural Language with Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can visual-semantic commonsense knowledge be inferred by blending videos and natural language captions, and how can a causal rationalization module be integrated to aid interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes iReason, a framework that infers visual-semantic commonsense knowledge using videos and natural language captions, and integrates a causal rationalization module for interpretability, outperforming state-of-the-art models.
papers.conclusion: iReason is an effective multimodal causal knowledge generation framework that outperforms existing models and offers interpretability through rationalization, with potential for improvement via better component models and more data.
papers.key_findings:
iReason outperforms VCC and language representation models (BERT, GPT-2) on causal reasoning tasks, particularly on Recall@1.
The canonical frame detection module enables video-native input and mines additional causal knowledge compared to randomly selected frames.
The causal rationalization module provides interpretability and aids error analysis.
Ablation studies show both visual and lingual context are important, with lingual context being more useful than visual context alone.
iReason's performance is dependent on the object detection and language representation models used.
papers.limitation:
iReason's performance is a function of the object detection module and the language representation model; using better ones could improve performance.
The iReasonData dataset, while effective, requires more data to cover additional causal interactions that humans easily infer.
future_direction: Using a better object detector and language representation model to improve context availability and event coding.
Expanding the dataset to cover more causal interactions.
papers.abstract: Causality knowledge is vital to building robust AI systems. Deep learning models often perform poorly on tasks that require causal reasoning, which is often derived using some form of commonsense knowledge not immediately available in the input but implicitly inferred by humans. Prior work has unraveled spurious observational biases that models fall prey to in the absence of causality. While language representation models preserve contextual knowledge within learned embeddings, they do not factor in causal relationships during training. By blending causal relationships with the input features to an existing model that performs visual cognition tasks (such as scene understanding, video captioning, video question-answering, etc.), better performance can be achieved owing to the insight causal relationships bring about. Recently, several models have been proposed that have tackled the task of mining causal data from either the visual or textual modality. However, there does not exist widespread research that mines causal relationships by juxtaposing the visual and language modalities. While images offer a rich and easy-to-process resource for us to mine causality knowledge from, videos are denser and consist of naturally time-ordered events. Also, textual information offers details that could be implicit in videos. We propose iReason, a framework that infers visual-semantic commonsense knowledge using both videos and natural language captions. Furthermore, iReason's architecture integrates a causal rationalization module to aid the process of interpretability, error analysis and bias detection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of iReason using a two-pronged comparative analysis with language representation learning models (BERT, GPT-2) as well as current state-of-the-art multimodal causality models.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Deep Generative Models via Causal Representation Learning
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces causal representation learning (CRL) from a statistical perspective, highlighting its connections to classical latent variable models and causal graphical models, and discusses identifiability results and open problems.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that causal representation learning is a promising approach for building interpretable deep generative models, but many open problems remain, including scalability, handling of confounders, and integration with foundation models.
future_direction: Scalability of CRL methods to large-scale models and data.
Handling of confounders and unobserved confounding.
Integration of CRL with foundation models like large language models.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in generative artificial intelligence (AI) rely on machine learning techniques such as deep learning and generative modeling to achieve state-of-the-art performance across wide-ranging domains. These methods' surprising performance is due in part to their ability to learn implicit "representations" of complex, multi-modal data. Unfortunately, deep neural networks are notoriously black boxes that obscure these representations, making them difficult to interpret or analyze. To resolve these difficulties, one approach is to build new interpretable neural network models from the ground up. This is the goal of the emerging field of causal representation learning (CRL) that uses causality as a vector for building flexible, interpretable, and transferable generative AI. CRL can be seen as a synthesis of three intrinsically statistical ideas: (i) latent variable models such as factor analysis; (ii) causal graphical models with latent variables; and (iii) nonparametric statistics and deep learning. This paper introduces CRL from a statistical perspective, focusing on connections to classical models as well as statistical and causal identifiability results. We also highlights key application areas, implementation strategies, and open statistical questions.

papers.title: Learning Causally Disentangled Representations via the Principle of Independent Causal Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How can we learn causally disentangled representations from data with causally related factors, using the principle of independent causal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ICM-VAE, a framework for learning causally disentangled representations using flow-based diffeomorphic causal mechanisms and a causal disentanglement prior, with theoretical identifiability guarantees up to permutation and elementwise reparameterization.
papers.conclusion: ICM-VAE effectively disentangles causal factors and mechanisms, as demonstrated theoretically and empirically on synthetic datasets, offering improved interventional robustness and counterfactual generation capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ICM-VAE achieves near-perfect disentanglement of causal factors (high DCI scores).
The model improves interventional robustness compared to baselines.
ICM-VAE generates consistent counterfactual images by intervening on latent causal variables.
The framework is compatible with general nonlinear structural causal models (SCMs).
Theoretical identifiability is proven under specified assumptions.
papers.limitation: Assumes the latent causal graph is known; causal discovery is not incorporated.
future_direction: Incorporate causal discovery to learn the causal graph from data.
Extend to settings with partially observed labels.
papers.abstract: Learning disentangled causal representations is a challenging problem that has gained significant attention recently due to its implications for extracting meaningful information for downstream tasks. In this work, we define a new notion of causal disentanglement from the perspective of independent causal mechanisms. We propose ICM-VAE, a framework for learning causally disentangled representations supervised by causally related observed labels. We model causal mechanisms using nonlinear learnable flow-based diffeomorphic functions to map noise variables to latent causal variables. Further, to promote the disentanglement of causal factors, we propose a causal disentanglement prior learned from auxiliary labels and the latent causal structure. We theoretically show the identifiability of causal factors and mechanisms up to permutation and elementwise reparameterization. We empirically demonstrate that our framework induces highly disentangled causal factors, improves interventional robustness, and is compatible with counterfactual generation.

papers.title: Inducing Causal World Models in LLMs for Zero-Shot Physical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we induce a causal world model in Large Language Models to improve zero-shot physical reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Causal World Model Induction (CWMI) framework, which augments a frozen LLM with a trainable Causal Physics Module and a Causal Intervention Loss to learn cause-and-effect relationships, significantly improving zero-shot physical reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Inducing an explicit causal world model within an LLM via the CWMI framework is a critical and effective step towards building AI systems with robust, generalizable physical reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
CWMI achieves 89.4% zero-shot accuracy on PIQA, outperforming Llama 3 8B (74.2%) and GPT-4 (85.5%).
On the novel PhysiCa-Bench, CWMI achieves 94.1% accuracy, 87.6% Causal Consistency Score, and a low Future State Prediction Error (MSE 0.08).
Ablation studies show the Causal Intervention Loss is critical for causal consistency, and the State Prediction Loss is necessary for grounding predictions in physical reality.
The two-component architecture (frozen LLM + trainable CPM) is more effective than fine-tuning the LLM directly, validating the modular design.
Performance scales with CPM capacity, plateauing at around 256M parameters for the rigid-body dynamics in the benchmark.
papers.limitation:
Struggles with complex multi-object interactions (e.g., a pile of falling blocks).
Cannot handle non-rigid and fluid dynamics, as training was on rigid-body physics.
Fails when key physical properties are not explicitly stated or strongly implied in the text (e.g., implicit understanding that a feather has high air resistance).
future_direction: Architectural enhancements to the CPM, such as adopting graph neural networks for multi-object tracking.
Incorporating physics-informed neural network techniques for continuous fields like fluids.
Integrating more sophisticated 3D visual representations.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their advanced linguistic capabilities, fundamentally lack an intuitive understanding of physical dynamics, which limits their effectiveness in real-world scenarios that require causal reasoning. In this paper, we introduce Causal World Model Induction (CWMI), a novel framework designed to embed an explicit model of causal physics within an LLM. Our approach incorporates a dedicated Causal Physics Module (CPM) and a new training objective called Causal Intervention Loss, encouraging the model to learn cause-and-effect relationships from multimodal data. By training the model to predict the outcomes of hypothetical interventions instead of merely capturing statistical correlations, CWMI develops a robust internal representation of physical laws. Experimental results show that CWMI significantly outperforms state-of-the-art LLMs on zero-shot physical reasoning tasks, including the PIQA benchmark and our newly proposed PhysiCa-Bench dataset. These findings demonstrate that inducing a causal world model is a critical step toward more reliable and generalizable AI systems.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Counterfactual reasoning: an analysis of in-context emergence
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning, i.e., predicting consequences of hypothetical scenarios by inferring unobserved latent concepts and copying contextual noise from factual observations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models are capable of in-context counterfactual reasoning, and through analysis of Transformers, finds that self-attention, model depth, and pre-training data diversity drive performance, with mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and that designated noise abduction heads emerge.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform counterfactual reasoning by leveraging self-attention and depth, and this ability extends to sequential data, suggesting potential for counterfactual story generation.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning on synthetic linear regression tasks.
Self-attention is crucial for counterfactual reasoning; MLP-only models fail.
Model depth improves counterfactual reasoning performance.
Pre-training data diversity improves performance and out-of-distribution generalization.
The latent parameter is linearly encoded in the residual stream, and designated noise abduction heads emerge in attention layers.
papers.limitation: The synthetic setup may not fully capture the complexity of natural language counterfactual reasoning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to natural language tasks and more complex functions.
Further exploration of the role of attention heads in counterfactual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit remarkable performance in in-context learning: the ability to learn and reason about the input context on the fly. This work studies in-context counterfactual reasoning in language models, that is, the ability to predict consequences of a hypothetical scenario. We focus on a well-defined, synthetic linear regression task that requires noise abduction. Accurate prediction is based on (1) inferring an unobserved latent concept and (2) copying contextual noise from factual observations. We show that language models are capable of counterfactual reasoning. Further, we enhance existing identifiability results and reduce counterfactual reasoning for a broad class of functions to a transformation on in-context observations. In Transformers, we find that self-attention, model depth and pre-training data diversity drive performance. Moreover, we provide mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and we introduce designated \textit{noise abduction heads} central to performing counterfactual reasoning. Lastly, our findings extend to counterfactual reasoning under SDE dynamics and reflect that Transformers can perform noise abduction on sequential data, providing preliminary evidence on the potential for counterfactual story generation. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/iccr.

papers.title: Automatically Identifying Local and Global Circuits with Linear Computation Graphs
papers.research_question: How to leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for fine-grained circuit analysis in Transformer language models without linear approximations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline using Sparse Autoencoders and Transcoders to refactor Transformer computation into a linear graph, enabling fine-grained circuit discovery without approximation via Hierarchical Attribution.
papers.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables fine-grained circuit analysis in Transformers, revealing detailed and beautiful internal structures that were previously obscured by coarser analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
The pipeline identifies fine-grained circuits for bracket matching, induction, and Indirect Object Identification (IOI) in GPT-2 Small.
SAE-based circuits reveal more detailed structural information than coarser head-level circuit analyses.
The IOI circuit differs at the feature level between two similar prompt templates (sJohn and sMary), showing nuanced mechanistic distinctions.
papers.limitation: The analysis is specific to certain inputs and might not generalize to other settings.
future_direction: Extending the method to extract more general circuits for abstract behaviors.
papers.abstract: Circuit analysis of any certain model behavior is a central task in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce our circuit discovery pipeline with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and a variant called Transcoders. With these two modules inserted into the model, the model's computation graph with respect to OV and MLP circuits becomes strictly linear. Our methods do not require linear approximation to compute the causal effect of each node. This fine-grained graph identifies both end-to-end and local circuits accounting for either logits or intermediate features. We can scalably apply this pipeline with a technique called Hierarchical Attribution. We analyze three kinds of circuits in GPT-2 Small: bracket, induction, and Indirect Object Identification circuits. Our results reveal new findings underlying existing discoveries.

papers.title: Missed Causes and Ambiguous Effects: Counterfactuals Pose Challenges for Interpreting Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What problems arise from using counterfactual theories of causality in neural network interpretability, specifically regarding overdetermination and the non-transitivity of counterfactual dependencies?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two key challenges in using counterfactual interventions for interpretability: overdetermination (redundant causes are missed) and the non-transitivity of counterfactual dependencies, which bias findings and complicate causal graph extraction.
papers.conclusion: Counterfactual theories of causality are sufficient for interpreting neural networks, but researchers must account for their pitfalls—non-transitivity and overdetermination—by using diverse data, multiple intervention types, and careful interpretation of causal graphs.
papers.key_findings:
Counterfactual dependencies in neural networks are generally not transitive, complicating the interpretation of causal chains.
Overdetermination (multiple sufficient causes) leads counterfactual methods to systematically miss certain causes, lowering recall.
Local causal dependencies (nodes that affect intermediate components but not the output directly) should be included in circuits to understand how abstractions are composed.
Using diverse datasets and both positive and negative counterfactuals can help mitigate these issues.
Counterfactual theories are still the most actionable for interpretability, but must be applied with awareness of their limitations.
future_direction: Use more diverse datasets and held-out evaluation sets to improve generalization of interpretability methods.
Employ both positive and negative counterfactuals (ablating and injecting activations) to capture redundant causes.
Create toy models with built-in overdetermination and preemption to develop and test methods that handle these challenges.
papers.abstract: Interpretability research takes counterfactual theories of causality for granted. Most causal methods rely on counterfactual interventions to inputs or the activations of particular model components, followed by observations of the change in models' output logits or behaviors. While this yields more faithful evidence than correlational methods, counterfactuals nonetheless have key problems that bias our findings in specific and predictable ways. Specifically, (i) counterfactual theories do not effectively capture multiple independently sufficient causes of the same effect, which leads us to miss certain causes entirely; and (ii) counterfactual dependencies in neural networks are generally not transitive, which complicates methods for extracting and interpreting causal graphs from neural networks. We discuss the implications of these challenges for interpretability researchers and propose concrete suggestions for future work.

papers.title: CARE: Turning LLMs Into Causal Reasoning Expert
papers.research_question: How can we enhance LLMs' causal reasoning ability to perform genuine causal discovery by integrating their world knowledge with outputs of causal discovery algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes CARE, a supervised fine-tuning framework that teaches LLMs to effectively integrate their world knowledge with the outputs of established causal discovery algorithms, enabling more accurate causal reasoning.
papers.conclusion: CARE enables LLMs to become effective causal reasoning experts by synergizing world knowledge and algorithmic outputs through targeted supervised fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs primarily rely on variable name semantics and ignore observational data when performing causal discovery.
Prompting LLMs with algorithm outputs does not improve and can sometimes degrade performance without fine-tuning.
The CARE framework, using SFT with data augmentation, enables LLMs to effectively integrate world knowledge and algorithmic evidence.
A fine-tuned Qwen2.5-1.5B model with CARE outperforms traditional causal discovery algorithms and larger LLMs.
The model shows robustness to variable name permutations, column reordering, and variable omission.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a 1.5B parameter model due to computational resources.
Scalability to extremely large and complex graphs (hundreds or thousands of variables) is not tested.
Resource considerations for SFT and data curation are practical challenges for adapting to new domains.
future_direction: Applying the CARE methodology to larger base LLMs (e.g., 7B, 70B).
Investigating scalability to problems with extremely large numbers of variables.
Managing computational costs and data curation for new, specialized domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated impressive capabilities across a range of reasoning and generation tasks. However, research studies have shown that LLMs lack the ability to identify causal relationships, a fundamental cornerstone of human intelligence. We first conduct an exploratory investigation of LLMs' behavior when asked to perform a causal-discovery task and find that they mostly rely on the semantic meaning of variable names, ignoring the observation data. This is unsurprising, given that LLMs were never trained to process structural datasets. To first tackle this challenge, we prompt the LLMs with the outputs of established causal discovery algorithms designed for observational datasets. These algorithm outputs effectively serve as the sufficient statistics of the observation data. However, quite surprisingly, we find that prompting the LLMs with these sufficient statistics decreases the LLMs' performance in causal discovery. To address this current limitation, we propose CARE, a framework that enhances LLMs' causal-reasoning ability by teaching them to effectively utilize the outputs of established causal-discovery algorithms through supervised fine-tuning. Experimental results show that a finetuned Qwen2.5-1.5B model produced by CARE significantly outperforms both traditional causal-discovery algorithms and state-of-the-art LLMs with over a thousand times more parameters, demonstrating effective utilization of its own knowledge and the external algorithmic clues.

papers.title: Neural Network Attributions: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: What is the causal effect of a particular input neuron on a particular output neuron of a neural network? The paper proposes a causal attribution method to answer this.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal attribution method for neural networks that computes the Average Causal Effect of input neurons on output neurons, satisfying key axioms and providing a global perspective.
papers.conclusion: The proposed causal attribution method provides meaningful attributions that align with domain knowledge and outperforms gradient-based methods like Integrated Gradients in identifying true causal factors.
papers.key_findings:
On the Iris dataset, the method reveals causal trends consistent with decision tree boundaries and data scatter plots.
On simulated sequence data, the method correctly identifies that the third feature is not causal, unlike Integrated Gradients which is biased by correlations.
On airplane anomaly detection, the method identifies causal factors (e.g., lateral acceleration) that agree with flight data recorder reports.
On a VAE with disentangled latents, the method correctly identifies latent dimensions that control rotation and scaling of digits.
The method satisfies axioms (ii)-(v) for attribution methods and avoids implicit biases present in gradient-based methods.
papers.limitation:
Assumes input neurons are not causally related, which is violated in RNNs with output-to-input connections.
Computing interventional expectations exactly can be costly for high-dimensional data, requiring approximations.
papers.abstract: We propose a new attribution method for neural networks developed using first principles of causality (to the best of our knowledge, the first such). The neural network architecture is viewed as a Structural Causal Model, and a methodology to compute the causal effect of each feature on the output is presented. With reasonable assumptions on the causal structure of the input data, we propose algorithms to efficiently compute the causal effects, as well as scale the approach to data with large dimensionality. We also show how this method can be used for recurrent neural networks. We report experimental results on both simulated and real datasets showcasing the promise and usefulness of the proposed algorithm.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Uncovering Intermediate Variables in Transformers using Circuit Probing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically uncover low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit probing, a method that combines probing and causal analysis to automatically uncover circuits computing hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Circuit probing provides a unified approach for a variety of analyses, combining and extending the capabilities of existing methods for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit probing can decipher the algorithms learned by models on simple arithmetic tasks.
Circuit probing reveals modular structure within a model, showing that shared and free variables are computed by distinct circuits.
Circuit probing tracks the development of circuits over training, showing circuit formation occurs continuously before generalization.
Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: Desiderata for Representation Learning: A Causal Perspective
papers.research_question: How can representation learning desiderata (non-spuriousness, efficiency, disentanglement) be formalized using causal notions, and how can metrics and algorithms be developed to learn such representations from single observational datasets?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a causal framework for representation learning that formalizes desiderata like non-spuriousness, efficiency, and disentanglement using counterfactual notions (probabilities of causation) and provides metrics and algorithms (CAUSAL-REP and IOSS) to learn such representations from single observational datasets.
papers.conclusion: Causality provides a fruitful perspective for representation learning, allowing intuitive desiderata to be formalized and leading to metrics and algorithms that can learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Non-spuriousness and efficiency in supervised representation learning can be formalized using probabilities of sufficiency (PS) and necessity (PN), leading to the CAUSAL-REP algorithm.
Disentanglement in unsupervised representation learning can be formalized via causal disentanglement, leading to the Independence-of-Support Score (IOSS) metric.
CAUSAL-REP learns non-spurious representations that improve out-of-distribution prediction on image and text datasets compared to baseline methods.
IOSS can distinguish disentangled from entangled representations better than existing unsupervised metrics on synthetic and real datasets.
The causal perspective enables the development of calculable metrics and algorithms for representation learning desiderata without requiring multiple environments or labeled features.
papers.limitation:
CAUSAL-REP requires the pinpointability condition (i.e., the unobserved common cause C can be pinpointed from X) for identification.
IOSS assumes compact support of the representation and may not apply to representations with unbounded support.
papers.abstract: Representation learning constructs low-dimensional representations to summarize essential features of high-dimensional data. This learning problem is often approached by describing various desiderata associated with learned representations; e.g., that they be non-spurious, efficient, or disentangled. It can be challenging, however, to turn these intuitive desiderata into formal criteria that can be measured and enhanced based on observed data. In this paper, we take a causal perspective on representation learning, formalizing non-spuriousness and efficiency (in supervised representation learning) and disentanglement (in unsupervised representation learning) using counterfactual quantities and observable consequences of causal assertions. This yields computable metrics that can be used to assess the degree to which representations satisfy the desiderata of interest and learn non-spurious and disentangled representations from single observational datasets.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Causation for Interpreting Neural Code Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the causal effect of software engineering properties (e.g., buggy code, comments) on Neural Code Model accuracy after controlling for hidden confounders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces docode, a post hoc interpretability method based on causal inference to explain predictions of Neural Code Models, and demonstrates its utility in detecting confounding bias.
papers.conclusion: docode is a useful method for detecting and facilitating the elimination of confounding bias in Neural Code Models.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of buggy code does not causally influence prediction performance despite observed correlations.
The presence of Type II Clones in training data causally impacts model effectiveness for certain programmatic constructs.
Strong correlations between the number of layers and performance were found to be spurious, with near-zero causal effects.
Masking random tokens has more impact on predictions than masking grammar-based categories for BERT-like models, suggesting incomplete capture of programming language structure.
papers.abstract: Neural Language Models of Code, or Neural Code Models (NCMs), are rapidly progressing from research prototypes to commercial developer tools. As such, understanding the capabilities and limitations of such models is becoming critical. However, the abilities of these models are typically measured using automated metrics that often only reveal a portion of their real-world performance. While, in general, the performance of NCMs appears promising, currently much is unknown about how such models arrive at decisions. To this end, this paper introduces $do_{code}$, a post hoc interpretability method specific to NCMs that is capable of explaining model predictions. $do_{code}$ is based upon causal inference to enable programming language-oriented explanations. While the theoretical underpinnings of $do_{code}$ are extensible to exploring different model properties, we provide a concrete instantiation that aims to mitigate the impact of spurious correlations by grounding explanations of model behavior in properties of programming languages. To demonstrate the practical benefit of $do_{code}$, we illustrate the insights that our framework can provide by performing a case study on two popular deep learning architectures and ten NCMs. The results of this case study illustrate that our studied NCMs are sensitive to changes in code syntax. All our NCMs, except for the BERT-like model, statistically learn to predict tokens related to blocks of code (\eg brackets, parenthesis, semicolon) with less confounding bias as compared to other programming language constructs. These insights demonstrate the potential of $do_{code}$ as a useful method to detect and facilitate the elimination of confounding bias in NCMs.

papers.title: Finding Alignments Between Interpretable Causal Variables and Distributed Neural Representations
papers.research_question: Can an interpretable symbolic algorithm be used to faithfully explain a complex neural network model? Specifically, how can we find alignments between interpretable causal variables and distributed neural representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces distributed alignment search (DAS), a method that uses gradient descent to find distributed alignments between high-level causal models and neural representations, overcoming limitations of brute-force search and localist alignments.
papers.conclusion: DAS removes previous obstacles to uncovering conceptual structure in trained neural nets and can discover internal structure that prior approaches miss.
papers.key_findings:
DAS finds perfect alignments (100% IIA) for both hierarchical equality and MoNLI tasks, showing the neural networks implement the high-level algorithms.
DAS outperforms brute-force search and localist alignment baselines in finding faithful alignments.
In the hierarchical equality task, the representation of equality is abstract and not decomposable into input identities, while in MoNLI, the entailment representation can be decomposed into word identities.
DAS can manipulate random network behavior only when the hidden representation is oversized, indicating it cannot construct entirely new behaviors from random structure.
The method reveals that distributed representations (non-standard bases) are crucial for finding interpretable alignments.
papers.limitation:
Scalability to large foundation models is limited because the rotation matrix size grows polynomially with hidden representation size.
The orthogonal matrix assumes linear transformation, which may not be optimal if the aligned variable is represented in a non-linear sub-manifold.
The optimization process stability depends on initialization, requiring multiple runs with different seeds.
Requires counterfactual data (base and source inputs) based on a causal graph.
future_direction: Investigate non-linear transformations (e.g., normalizing flows) for alignment.
Explore better initialization schemes for the rotation matrix.
Scale to large models by using low-rank approximations of the rotation matrix.
papers.abstract: Causal abstraction is a promising theoretical framework for explainable artificial intelligence that defines when an interpretable high-level causal model is a faithful simplification of a low-level deep learning system. However, existing causal abstraction methods have two major limitations: they require a brute-force search over alignments between the high-level model and the low-level one, and they presuppose that variables in the high-level model will align with disjoint sets of neurons in the low-level one. In this paper, we present distributed alignment search (DAS), which overcomes these limitations. In DAS, we find the alignment between high-level and low-level models using gradient descent rather than conducting a brute-force search, and we allow individual neurons to play multiple distinct roles by analyzing representations in non-standard bases-distributed representations. Our experiments show that DAS can discover internal structure that prior approaches miss. Overall, DAS removes previous obstacles to conducting causal abstraction analyses and allows us to find conceptual structure in trained neural nets.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Do learned representations respect causal relationships?
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether learned attribute-specific representations respect the same causal relations as the underlying attributes, and to what extent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces NCINet, a learning-based method for observational causal discovery from high-dimensional representations, and shows that learned representations can respect the causal relations between attributes, with consistency correlated to predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that learned representations can respect causal relationships under controlled scenarios, and introduces NCINet, which outperforms existing methods for causal discovery from high-dimensional representations.
papers.key_findings:
NCINet significantly outperforms existing observational causal discovery approaches on synthetic and real data.
Under controlled scenarios, learned representations can satisfy the same causal relations as the underlying attribute labels.
The causal consistency between representations and labels is positively correlated with the predictive capability of the representations.
Causal consistency degrades with overfitting of the attribute predictors.
The adversarial loss component in NCINet improves its generalization ability.
papers.abstract: Data often has many semantic attributes that are causally associated with each other. But do attribute-specific learned representations of data also respect the same causal relations? We answer this question in three steps. First, we introduce NCINet, an approach for observational causal discovery from high-dimensional data. It is trained purely on synthetically generated representations and can be applied to real representations, and is specifically designed to mitigate the domain gap between the two. Second, we apply NCINet to identify the causal relations between image representations of different pairs of attributes with known and unknown causal relations between the labels. For this purpose, we consider image representations learned for predicting attributes on the 3D Shapes, CelebA, and the CASIA-WebFace datasets, which we annotate with multiple multi-class attributes. Third, we analyze the effect on the underlying causal relation between learned representations induced by various design choices in representation learning. Our experiments indicate that (1) NCINet significantly outperforms existing observational causal discovery approaches for estimating the causal relation between pairs of random samples, both in the presence and absence of an unobserved confounder, (2) under controlled scenarios, learned representations can indeed satisfy the underlying causal relations between their respective labels, and (3) the causal relations are positively correlated with the predictive capability of the representations.

papers.title: LLM Interpretability with Identifiable Temporal-Instantaneous Representation
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable temporal and instantaneous causal representations from LLM activations with theoretical guarantees?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a temporal causal representation learning framework for LLM interpretability that captures time-delayed and instantaneous causal relations with theoretical guarantees.
papers.conclusion: The proposed temporal causal representation learning framework provides a principled way to uncover temporal and instantaneous causal structures in LLM activations, offering a step toward more interpretable and controllable language models.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully discovers meaningful concept relationships in LLM activations by extending sparse autoencoder techniques.
Modeling both temporal and instantaneous conceptual relationships advances the interpretability of LLMs.
The method provides theoretical guarantees for identifiability under linear assumptions and sparsity constraints.
It demonstrates efficacy on synthetic datasets scaled to real-world complexity and on activations from real LLMs.
The approach offers a principled way to uncover causal structures in LLM activations.
papers.limitation: The linearity assumption may not hold in practice, and the scalability to very high-dimensional spaces is limited by the need to estimate large matrices.
future_direction: Extending the framework to nonlinear models.
Scaling the approach to larger models and higher-dimensional spaces.
Incorporating domain knowledge to guide the discovery of causal structures.
papers.abstract: Despite Large Language Models' remarkable capabilities, understanding their internal representations remains challenging. Mechanistic interpretability tools such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were developed to extract interpretable features from LLMs but lack temporal dependency modeling, instantaneous relation representation, and more importantly theoretical guarantees, undermining both the theoretical foundations and the practical confidence necessary for subsequent analyses. While causal representation learning (CRL) offers theoretically grounded approaches for uncovering latent concepts, existing methods cannot scale to LLMs' rich conceptual space due to inefficient computation. To bridge the gap, we introduce an identifiable temporal causal representation learning framework specifically designed for LLMs' high-dimensional concept space, capturing both time-delayed and instantaneous causal relations. Our approach provides theoretical guarantees and demonstrates efficacy on synthetic datasets scaled to match real-world complexity. By extending SAE techniques with our temporal causal framework, we successfully discover meaningful concept relationships in LLM activations. Our findings show that modeling both temporal and instantaneous conceptual relationships advances the interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: How Transformers Learn Causal Structure with Gradient Descent
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn causal structure with gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that gradient descent on a two-layer transformer learns causal structure by encoding the latent causal graph in the first attention layer, with the gradient of the attention matrix encoding mutual information between tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformers learn causal structure by encoding the causal graph in the first attention layer through gradient descent, with the gradient encoding mutual information.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient descent on a two-layer transformer learns to encode the latent causal graph in the first attention layer.
The gradient of the attention matrix encodes mutual information between tokens, and the largest entries correspond to edges in the causal graph.
For in-context Markov chains, transformers learn an induction head.
Empirically, transformers trained on the task recover a wide variety of causal structures.
For multiple parents, transformers can distribute the causal graph across multiple attention heads.
papers.abstract: The incredible success of transformers on sequence modeling tasks can be largely attributed to the self-attention mechanism, which allows information to be transferred between different parts of a sequence. Self-attention allows transformers to encode causal structure which makes them particularly suitable for sequence modeling. However, the process by which transformers learn such causal structure via gradient-based training algorithms remains poorly understood. To better understand this process, we introduce an in-context learning task that requires learning latent causal structure. We prove that gradient descent on a simplified two-layer transformer learns to solve this task by encoding the latent causal graph in the first attention layer. The key insight of our proof is that the gradient of the attention matrix encodes the mutual information between tokens. As a consequence of the data processing inequality, the largest entries of this gradient correspond to edges in the latent causal graph. As a special case, when the sequences are generated from in-context Markov chains, we prove that transformers learn an induction head (Olsson et al., 2022). We confirm our theoretical findings by showing that transformers trained on our in-context learning task are able to recover a wide variety of causal structures.

papers.title: CNRL at SemEval-2020 Task 5: Modelling Causal Reasoning in Language with Multi-Head Self-Attention Weights Based Counterfactual Detection
papers.research_question: How can we model causal reasoning in natural language by detecting counterfactuals using multi-head self-attention weights from transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an approach for counterfactual detection and antecedent-consequent span detection using multi-head self-attention weights from transformer models, with a shared base architecture for knowledge sharing between the two sub-tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach using multi-head self-attention weights is effective for counterfactual detection and span detection, and attention heads exhibit linguistically selective attention with respect to the conditional nature of counterfactual statements.
papers.key_findings:
RoBERTa performs best for the counterfactual detection sub-task, while BERT performs best for the antecedent-consequent detection sub-task.
DistilBERT, a smaller model, shows comparable performance to larger models for both sub-tasks.
Attention heads become specialized to attend to specific linguistic features (e.g., punctuation, auxiliary verbs, conjunctions) related to the conditional nature of counterfactual statements.
The proposed regression-based approach effectively detects antecedent-consequent spans in counterfactual statements.
The model differentiates causal connectives from non-causal ones in text.
papers.limitation: Treating antecedent-consequent detection as a regression task does not monitor Exact Match score, which is more significant for token-level sequence labeling approaches.
future_direction: Post-inference processing on the predicted spans
Replacing the regression module with a token-level sequence labelling module
papers.abstract: In this paper, we describe an approach for modelling causal reasoning in natural language by detecting counterfactuals in text using multi-head self-attention weights. We use pre-trained transformer models to extract contextual embeddings and self-attention weights from the text. We show the use of convolutional layers to extract task-specific features from these self-attention weights. Further, we describe a fine-tuning approach with a common base model for knowledge sharing between the two closely related sub-tasks for counterfactual detection. We analyze and compare the performance of various transformer models in our experiments. Finally, we perform a qualitative analysis with the multi-head self-attention weights to interpret our models' dynamics.

papers.title: Interpretability at Scale: Identifying Causal Mechanisms in Alpaca
papers.research_question: How can we scale causal interpretability methods to large language models to faithfully understand their internal mechanisms, and what causal mechanisms does Alpaca use for a numerical reasoning task?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Boundless DAS, a method that scales causal interpretability to large language models by replacing brute-force search with learned parameters, and uses it to show that Alpaca implements a simple causal model with interpretable boolean variables for a numerical reasoning task.
papers.conclusion: Boundless DAS is a step towards understanding the internal causal mechanisms of large language models, and Alpaca uses interpretable algorithmic structure for the task.
papers.key_findings:
Boundless DAS can efficiently search for interpretable causal structure in large language models.
Alpaca solves the Price Tagging task by implementing a causal model with two interpretable boolean variables (left and right boundary checks).
The alignment of neural representations with these variables is robust to changes in inputs and instructions.
Only a small fraction (5-10%) of the representation space is needed to align each causal variable.
The found alignments are not due to random structure, as shown by comparisons with random models.
papers.limitation:
Failure to find causal structure with Boundless DAS is not a proof that such structure is missing, because the method is not completely exhaustive and the space of causal models tested is limited.
For models where task accuracy is below 100%, IIA is constrained by task performance.
future_direction: Tighten the connection by modeling errors in the language model in more detail.
Involve humans in the loop for testing different hypotheses of the high-level causal model.
Apply Boundless DAS to larger LLMs with stronger reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Obtaining human-interpretable explanations of large, general-purpose language models is an urgent goal for AI safety. However, it is just as important that our interpretability methods are faithful to the causal dynamics underlying model behavior and able to robustly generalize to unseen inputs. Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) is a powerful gradient descent method grounded in a theory of causal abstraction that has uncovered perfect alignments between interpretable symbolic algorithms and small deep learning models fine-tuned for specific tasks. In the present paper, we scale DAS significantly by replacing the remaining brute-force search steps with learned parameters -- an approach we call Boundless DAS. This enables us to efficiently search for interpretable causal structure in large language models while they follow instructions. We apply Boundless DAS to the Alpaca model (7B parameters), which, off the shelf, solves a simple numerical reasoning problem. With Boundless DAS, we discover that Alpaca does this by implementing a causal model with two interpretable boolean variables. Furthermore, we find that the alignment of neural representations with these variables is robust to changes in inputs and instructions. These findings mark a first step toward faithfully understanding the inner-workings of our ever-growing and most widely deployed language models. Our tool is extensible to larger LLMs and is released publicly at `https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyvene`.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Learning to Focus: Causal Attention Distillation via Gradient-Guided Token Pruning
papers.research_question: How do distracting patterns (confounding tokens) in training data misdirect model attention during inference, and how can we mitigate this to improve reasoning accuracy and generation quality?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a two-stage framework (LeaF) that identifies and prunes confounding tokens via gradient-guided comparison with a teacher model, then distills causal attention to improve the student model's focus on critical information, leading to enhanced reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: LeaF effectively identifies and eliminates confounding tokens, enabling student models to capture more reliable causal dependencies and achieve substantial improvements in accuracy and robustness across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and multi-hop QA benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning confounding tokens from training data significantly improves reasoning accuracy (over 20% on math, over 10% on code) without additional training.
LeaF consistently outperforms standard knowledge distillation across math, code, and multi-hop QA benchmarks.
Response-level pruning (in addition to instruction-level) yields further performance gains, indicating distracting patterns exist in both instructions and generated responses.
